title: ropeway:handbook-title-50
text: An aerial ropeway carries a cabin across ground you would rather not walk. A haul rope is strung from tower to tower, the cabin hangs from it on a jaw clamped round the rope, and it runs end to end and back again. It carries two people, or two loads of freight, or one of each - a basket or a chest straps onto either bench, which is what these lines were mostly built to do. The words Tower - the gantry you build. Every tower is the same structure; a tower with only one span attached is an end tower, and that is where the cabin stops. There is no separate station block. Span - one straight stretch of haul rope between two towers. Line - all the towers and spans chained end to end. Footing - the pylon footing on the ground. It is the tower: it validates the build, owns the spans and takes every click. Sheave - the split housing in the pylon head that the rope runs through, four blocks above the footing. Its two cheeks leave a slot down the middle, and the cabin's hanger rides up that slot. Drive housing - the machine that turns the haul rope. It stands within eight blocks of any tower on the line and an axle runs into any of its four sides. The eight blocks are measured through the air, so it may sit on the ground beside the footing or up level with a windmill's axle, whichever the mill needs. It turns the line of whichever footing is nearest it that is already part of a line, and only that one, so where two lines pass close together each wants its own. A lone footing standing on its own is not a line yet and is passed over. A line with none does not move. Optional, and one is enough. Bullwheel - a spoked wheel you may put on a tower's crossarm in place of the pylon head. It is decoration: it drives nothing, and it turns whenever the line is running, so you can see from a distance that the drive is working. Jaw - the clamp at the top of the hanger, closed on the rope itself at sheave height. Station rail - the pair of bars hanging under the crossarm, three blocks long and flared open at both ends. The cabin's guide rollers run inside them. Building a tower Place a pylon footing on the ground where the tower should stand. It turns to face you, and the whole tower is measured up from it. Look at the placed footing - while the tower is unfinished the block info panel names the two directions the cabin will pass through, so you can turn the footing down the line before building anything. You then place fifteen more blocks by hand: - Two posts of four blocks, standing on the ground three blocks either side of the footing. Wood or dressed stone: logs, debarked logs, planks, raw stone, cobblestone, drystone, polished rock or stone bricks, so the tower can match whatever you build in. Slabs, stairs and soil are not posts. - A seven-wide crossarm across their tops, four blocks up: the pylon head directly above the footing with three ropeway braces either side of it. The two outermost braces are what make the archway five wide rather than three, and that width is what stops the cabin catching a post where the line changes direction. They are not free: six braces is two crafts, so a tower costs two metal plates instead of one, on every tower of a long route. That is the whole tower - one crossarm, one block deep. It leaves a clear five-wide, four-tall archway, and the cabin threads through it nose first, its hanger up between the sheave cheeks and its jaw closed on the rope. Right-click the footing at any time. If the tower is unfinished it tells you how many blocks are missing and lights up every cell that is wrong or empty - red where the wrong block sits, and the colour of the block it wants where nothing is. Every other click a tower takes lands on the footing too; the pylon head up top is only a piece of the frame. Sneak and right-click the footing to open the tower guide: the build order in words, next to a turning 3D view of the blocks a tower is made of, the two drive blocks and the cabin itself. Next: Building a Line, then Power and the Drive.
